problem: Navigation agents pre-trained in noiseless simulators degrade sharply under real actuation and odometry noise. Adapting them needs ground-truth poses or explicit noise models (as in domain randomization), which are unavailable and slow to fit in deployment.
motivation: Custom robots have unlimited combinations of motors and sensors, so noise cannot be modeled exhaustively and GT poses cannot be collected in the real world. In modular agents, only the observation (mapping and localization) module needs adapting, and the global map it produces gives a free self-supervision signal because errors accumulate over time.
key_idea: Drive the agent on a round-trip trajectory and fine-tune the localization module so that the global map built from scratch on the backward path matches the forward-path reference map (stop-gradient MSE), with no GT pose.
insight: Consistency of overlapping global maps is tightly coupled to pose accuracy, so it works as a label-free pose supervision signal. The ablations show that step-wise loss over the whole backward path matters (last-step only gives 0.15 m / 2.57° vs 0.03 m / 0.36°), MSE beats BCE (BCE gives noisy, high-variance gradients), and random-crop augmentation helps (0.06 vs 0.03 m). Pose error is kept similar across the forward and backward paths, which justifies using the earlier, more accurate forward map as the target.
method: Modular agent: Active Neural SLAM style mapping and localization module f_θ (egocentric map + pose estimate, fused into a global occupancy map) plus a separate planner π_ψ; only the localization part of f_θ is fine-tuned, the policy is kept frozen.
Round-trip data: run any navigation for t_r steps, turn 180°, and execute the reversed action sequence; the forward path builds the reference map M_F.
Backward map: at t_r+1 the agent resets its map and builds a new M_{B,t} from scratch, but keeps the same global coordinate frame via full odometry s_{1:t}.
Global map consistency loss: L = sum over backward steps of ||stopgrad(M_F) − M_{B,t}||_2 (MSE), applied at every backward step.
Random-crop augmentation: sample t1<t_o<t2 within a trajectory, build the reference map from t1..t_o and the backward maps from t_o+1..t2, giving many overlapping sub-round-trips.
Noise models for the unseen domain: LoCoBot-derived actuation noise (constant and stochastic motion bias, motion drift) and Gaussian-mixture odometry noise with severity k.
Test-time adaptation: fine-tune in a single unseen scene with only 20 trajectories, taking 2.5 minutes.

setting.backbone: Active Neural SLAM agent (mapper and pose estimator CNNs, pre-trained noiseless, localization part fine-tuned self-supervised)
setting.training_data: Pre-trained on noiseless Gibson (72 train scenes); fine-tuned with 160 self-collected 100-step round-trip trajectories (no labels); 20 trajectories for test-time adaptation
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + noisy odometry sensor reading
setting.action_space: discrete: Forward, Turn Left, Turn Right
setting.simulator: Habitat (Gibson scenes) with LoCoBot-based actuation/odometry noise models
setting.privileged: none at adaptation/test time (GT poses only used for evaluation and for the GT-Train upper bound)

numbers.backbone: Active Neural SLAM, localization fine-tuned self-supervised

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmarks; only custom exploration/localization/mapping evaluation on Gibson in Habitat. Some results (noise severity, path length) are in figures only.
results: Self-supervised adaptation cuts localization error from 0.15 m / 2.67° (no adaptation) to 0.03 m / 0.36° and raises exploration coverage from 82.02% to 91.79%, beating domain randomization (89.06%, 0.12 m) while training in 5 min vs 65 min. It approaches the GT-supervised upper bound (93.75%), and in test-time adaptation with 20 trajectories it slightly exceeds GT training on coverage (92.25% vs 91.06%).
limitations: Evaluated only on exploration with Active Neural SLAM in simulation with synthetic noise models; no real-robot experiments and no goal-conditioned tasks
Assumes round-trip trajectories with overlapping observations and that forward-path error is smaller than backward-path error; benefit diminishes for longer trajectories
Only the localization module is fine-tuned; visual (mapping) domain shift is not addressed
